archetype.name: Improviser (sack-prone)
archetype.definition: A veteran who extends plays and hunts downfield. His throws beyond 10 yards and his scrambles drive the offense, and the time he holds the ball turns too many dropbacks into sacks.

report.headline: The throws are good again; the sacks erase them, and a concussion pauses everything.
report.take:
This is a better version of Watson than any of his Browns seasons. His 7.25 yards per attempt and 65.5% completion rate are well above the 5.32 and 63.4% he posted in 2024, and his passing yards per game rank 18th of 49. When he actually gets the ball out, the results are positive at every depth past the line of scrimmage: +0.105 EPA on short throws, +0.466 on intermediate and +0.419 on deep. His throws of 10+ air yards added up to +29 EPA. Throw away the sacks and this is a solidly above-average passer.

You can't throw away the sacks. An 11.7% sack rate ranks 44th of 49 and is on a 70-sack pace, and it's the single reason all of that positive throwing nets to a dropback EPA total of -0.8. Two forces feed it. Cleveland's offense ranks 32nd of 32 in hit rate allowed, so the protection is the worst in the league. Watson also converts 41.8% of pressures into sacks. That isn't new: his pressure-to-sack rank has sat around 39th-48th in nearly every season on record, and 67th of 68 in 2022. It is the cost of the same instinct that produces his best plays. He holds the ball looking for the shot, and scrambles pay +0.433 EPA apiece with 9 first downs. The bill comes due on third down, where he sees 8.4 yards to go on average, converts 28.4% and took 10 sacks for -0.184 EPA a play.

The numbers also hide some bad luck in the scoring column. A 2.8% TD rate ranks 38th, yet his red-zone CPOE is +6.6 and his downfield passing is efficient, so touchdowns should come more often than they have. The last three games produced zero passing TDs despite 265 yards a game. The fumbles are a real cost, not just noise: 3 lost rank 45th, and seven turnover-worthy fumbles suggest the ball security issue goes beyond bounce luck. That fits a QB who takes this many hits. Designed runs have also been a dead end, at -0.399 EPA with a 35% stuff rate behind a rushing offense that ranks 29th.

The direction has tilted the wrong way. Over the last five games his EPA per dropback fell to -0.062, and over the last three to -0.075, even as yardage rose. Volume is up and efficiency is down, the profile of a QB moving the ball between the 20s and then giving it back with sacks and stalled drives. Now a concussion has him out, and Shedeur Sanders started Week 9.

strengths.title: Downfield throws are winning plays
strengths.body: On throws of 10+ air yards he's at +0.446 EPA a play with 4 TDs and 1 INT, and the intermediate window is his best area. That fits the career-long profile of a QB whose value has always come from aggressive throws rather than volume. It should hold as long as the protection gives him time to reach the second read.

strengths.title: Scrambles turn broken plays positive
strengths.body: His 24 scrambles average +0.433 EPA and produced 9 first downs. They are the upside of his habit of holding the ball. His rushing yards still rank 5th among QBs, though the designed-run game hasn't helped, and the scrambles partly pay back what the sacks cost.

strengths.title: Accurate short game, few interceptions
strengths.body: He's completing 73.3% on short throws with positive CPOE. His 1.2% INT rate is better than the league's 2.4%. He feeds Harold Fannin Jr. well (+0.34 EPA a target), and the floor of the passing game is sound.

concerns.title: Sacks wipe out the passing value
concerns.body: An 11.7% sack rate (44th) behind the league's worst hit-rate protection drags his dropback EPA below zero. His pressure-to-sack rate has been poor every season, so this is partly who he is and partly a line that can't hold up. Both are unlikely to fix themselves midseason. Games like the 8-sack outings against the Jets and Steelers are the floor.

concerns.title: Third downs stall out
concerns.body: Long yardage plus sacks makes third down his worst situation, at -0.184 EPA, a 28.4% conversion rate and negative CPOE. Weak early-down rushing puts him in these spots, and his tendency to hold the ball makes them worse.

concerns.title: Fumbles and a recent efficiency slide
concerns.body: Three lost fumbles rank 45th, and seven turnover-worthy fumbles say it's more than luck. Over the last three games, efficiency has slipped to -0.075 EPA per dropback with no passing TDs.

trend.note: He opened with positive-EPA games against Tampa Bay and Pittsburgh in Weeks 2 and 4, then has been negative in three of the last four. Yardage climbed late (308 and 324 in Weeks 7-8) while sacks and empty red-zone trips sank the efficiency.

nextGame.headline: Ruled out with a concussion; Houston's pass rush awaits his return
nextGame.body:
Watson is listed Out with a concussion as of November 9, and Shedeur Sanders already started Week 9, so the expectation is that he doesn't play against Houston. If he were cleared, the matchup would cut both ways. Houston generates sacks at the second-highest rate in the league and ranks 7th in hit rate, which is exactly the pressure his profile handles worst behind a line that ranks last in hits allowed. But Houston also gives up the most explosive passes in the league and ranks 24th against deep throws, the area where his downfield efficiency lives.

On Houston's side, safety Reed Blankenship (86% of snaps) is out with his own concussion, which would further soften the deep middle. Cleveland reports no offensive injuries beyond Watson. The Book has Cleveland as a 4.5-point home underdog with a 39.5 total, a low-scoring script that points to a heavier passing load for whoever starts. It's an early forecast, but nothing in it should affect the game.

keyMatchups.title: Houston's sack rate against his holding
keyMatchups.body: Houston's 9.2% sack rate ranks 2nd, and Cleveland allows the most hits in the league. For a QB who turns 41.8% of pressures into sacks, this is the defining fight of any game against this front.

keyMatchups.title: Big plays are there to take
keyMatchups.body: Houston ranks last in explosive pass rate allowed and 24th in deep EPA, and it's without Blankenship. A QB who hangs in for the shot could hit big if the protection holds long enough.

keyMatchups.title: Tight end lane narrows
keyMatchups.body: Fannin has been his most efficient target, but Houston has held lead tight ends 3 points under their averages (3rd best) while giving up the most to WR2s. Volume would likely shift to the receivers.

nextGame.watch: Whether he clears the concussion protocol; if not, Shedeur Sanders gets a second straight start against a top-two pass rush.

restOfSeason.body:
When he returns, expect the same shape: good yardage at a per-attempt rate above league average, very few interceptions, and sack totals that keep his overall efficiency near or below zero. The sack problem is structural, a career-long pressure-to-sack tendency behind the league's leakiest protection, so don't project a fix. The touchdown rate is the part most likely to move up, given how well his intermediate and deep throws grade and his positive red-zone accuracy. I'd expect roughly 1 to 1.5 TDs a game rather than the near-zero of his recent stretch.

The bigger unknown is availability and the job itself. A concussion with a backup already starting adds risk to every week. His rushing should keep adding a useful floor through scrambles even if designed runs stay ineffective.
swingFactors: Concussion recovery and whether Shedeur Sanders keeps the job
Pass protection: any improvement from last in hit rate
TD rate regressing toward his downfield efficiency

confidence.note: The eight-start profile is consistent with his career sack tendencies, but the concussion and a backup already starting cloud his availability.
